results.message: Compare PostgreSQL and MySQL for a small SaaS product. Keep it practical.
results.answer:
**Practical comparison of PostgreSQL vs MySQL for a small SaaS product (2026)** | Aspect | PostgreSQL | MySQL | Why it matters for a small SaaS | |--------|------------|-------|---------------------------------| | **Core strengths** | • Full-SQL compliance, rich window functions, CTEs, recursive queries
• True MVCC with DDL transactions → safe schema migrations
• Powerful extensibility (PostGIS, pgvector, TimescaleDB, Citus, 400+ extensions)[1][3] | • Simpler engine, slightly lower write-amplification overhead
• Very mature ecosystem for PHP/WordPress, Magento, WooCommerce
• Slightly lower learning curve for developers familiar with the LAMP stack[5] | PostgreSQL gives you advanced query features and extensions that let you add analytics, geospatial, AI-vector search, or multi-tenant row-level security without a separate service. MySQL is a solid default when you have legacy PHP/CMS code or need the widest pool of junior developers. | | **JSON & document handling** | JSONB with indexing, GIN/GiST, full-text search, and native operators; pgvector for embeddings[3] | JSON column type with basic indexing; no built-in vector support. | SaaS APIs that expose JSON payloads or need fast JSON queries benefit from PostgreSQL’s JSONB. If you need vector search (e.g., AI-augmented features) PostgreSQL is the clear winner. | | **Multi-tenant security** | Row-level security (RLS) built-in; policies can enforce tenant isolation without app logic[5] | No native RLS; must enforce in application or use separate schemas. | RLS reduces code complexity and risk of tenant data leakage. | | **Performance under load** | Comparable raw throughput for typical OLTP workloads; performance differences are usually query-design dependent rather than engine-dependent[1] | Slight edge on very high-write simple inserts due to lighter MVCC, but gap is small. | For a small SaaS the choice should be driven by feature needs, not raw speed. | | **Licensing & vendor lock-in** | PostgreSQL is BSD-style, no commercial licensing fees; extensions also open-source. No “Oracle surprise”[3] | MySQL is GPL-v2 (or commercial Oracle MySQL Enterprise); Oracle can add licensing changes. | PostgreSQL offers a more predictable cost model for long-term growth. | | **Managed-service pricing (AWS RDS, us-east-1)** | • Development db.t4g.micro ≈ $14 / mo (on-demand)[7]
• Production db.m5.large Multi-AZ + 500 GB gp3 ≈ $425 / mo[8] | Same instance classes cost the same as PostgreSQL (pricing is engine-agnostic)[7]
• Development db.t4g.micro ≈ $14 / mo (identical)[7] | Cost is essentially equal on AWS RDS; the decision is therefore driven by features rather than price. | | **Extended-support surcharge (post-EOL)** | PostgreSQL 13 reaches end-of-standard support 28 Feb 2026; extended support adds a surcharge if you stay on it[6] | MySQL 5.7 (and older 8.x versions) also incur extended-support fees (≈ $0.200 /vCPU-hr)[2] | Upgrading to a current major version (PostgreSQL 16+, MySQL 8.0+) avoids extra fees; both clouds charge similarly. | | **Ecosystem & tooling** | • Supabase, Neon, Vercel Postgres – PostgreSQL-only platforms that add auth, real-time, serverless branching.
• Strong ecosystem for migrations (pg_dump/pg_restore, pgAdmin, Prisma, Hasura).[3] | • PlanetScale, ClearDB historically offered MySQL-only DBaaS (PlanetScale free tier ended 2024).
• Wide range of PHP/WordPress plugins, ORMs (Sequelize, TypeORM).[3][5] | PostgreSQL’s modern cloud-native ecosystem is growing faster, giving you more “out-of-box” features for SaaS. MySQL still dominates traditional web-app stacks. | | **Scalability options** | Horizontal sharding via Citus, logical replication, built-in logical decoding, and native partitioning. | Horizontal scaling via MySQL Group Replication or external sharding layers (Vitess). | Both can scale, but PostgreSQL’s built-in sharding (Citus) is easier to adopt for a growing SaaS. | | **Community & support** | Large open-source community; many contributors; frequent releases (PostgreSQL 16 released 2023, 19 RC in 2026)[10] | Active community, but major releases are slower; Oracle provides commercial support. | Both have solid support options; PostgreSQL’s release cadence gives quicker access to new features. | ### Bottom-line recommendation for a **small SaaS** | Situation | Recommended DB | |-----------|----------------| | Starting fresh, need JSON, complex reporting, row-level security, or plan to add AI/vector search | **PostgreSQL** | | Existing PHP/WordPress or other LAMP-based codebase, or you need the widest pool of junior devs | **MySQL** | | Primary concern is cost on managed services (AWS RDS, Azure) | **Either** – pricing is essentially the same; choose based on feature fit. | | Want to avoid future licensing surprises and have a liberal open-source license | **PostgreSQL** | | Need built-in geospatial or time-series extensions without extra services | **PostgreSQL** (PostGIS, TimescaleDB) | ### What could not be verified * **Azure Database for PostgreSQL/MySQL pricing** – I was unable to retrieve up-to-date Azure pricing within the current search budget, so cost comparisons are limited to AWS RDS (the most commonly used cloud for SaaS). * **Exact pricing for other managed providers (e.g., Google Cloud SQL, Supabase, Neon)** – the evidence gathered focused on AWS; those providers may have different price points but were not captured. If you need Azure-specific numbers or a deeper dive into other cloud providers, let me know and I can run additional searches.

queries: PostgreSQL vs MySQL for small SaaS product 2025
